turns.user: why does my sql count come out wrong when i join two tables. orders and order_items, i do select count(*) from orders o join order_items i on o.id=i.order_id and it gives way more than the number of orders
turns.assistant:
Because it's a one-to-many join. Each order can have several items, so the join produces one row per item, and COUNT(*) counts those rows, not orders.

If an order has 3 items, it shows up 3 times in the result. To count orders, use COUNT(DISTINCT o.id). Or if you just want the number of orders, you don't need the join at all: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders.

turns.user: ok makes sense. but what if i want orders and the total number of items per order
turns.assistant:
Group by the order and count the items:

SELECT o.id, COUNT(i.id) AS item_count
FROM orders o
LEFT JOIN order_items i ON o.id = i.order_id
GROUP BY o.id;

The GROUP BY collapses the repeated order rows into one per order, and COUNT(i.id) counts the items in each group. I used LEFT JOIN so orders with no items still show up, with a count of 0. With a plain JOIN they'd be dropped.

turns.user: why count(i.id) and not count(*) there
turns.assistant:
Because of the LEFT JOIN. For an order with no items, the join still gives one row, with NULLs for all the item columns. COUNT(*) counts that row and returns 1, which is wrong. COUNT(i.id) only counts non-null values, so it returns 0.

Rule of thumb: COUNT(*) counts rows, COUNT(column) counts non-null values in that column, COUNT(DISTINCT column) counts unique non-null values.

turns.user: and if i want sum of revenue per customer, orders has customer_id and total, would joining items mess that up too
turns.assistant:
Yes, if you join to items and then sum o.total, each order's total gets repeated once per item, so revenue is inflated. It's the same issue.

Simplest fix: don't join items at all if the total is on orders:

SELECT customer_id, SUM(total) AS revenue
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id;

If you need item level data too, aggregate items in a subquery or CTE first (one row per order), then join that to orders. Or sum from the items table directly (quantity * price) so each row is counted once.

turns.user: got it. so basically aggregate before joining when its one to many?
turns.assistant:
Mostly yes. If you need to combine data from two tables with a one-to-many relationship, collapse the many side to one row per key first, then join. That way you can't multiply rows.

Example:

WITH item_counts AS (
  SELECT order_id, COUNT(*) AS n
  FROM order_items
  GROUP BY order_id
)
SELECT o.customer_id, SUM(o.total), SUM(c.n)
FROM orders o
LEFT JOIN item_counts c ON c.order_id = o.id
GROUP BY o.customer_id;

Now each order appears exactly once in the join.
